title: New Criticism & Formalism
description: Close reading, the text alone, the intentional fallacy

concepts.title: The New Criticism
concepts.contentHtml:
New Criticism dominated American literary study from the 1930s through the 1960s. Its central figures — John Crowe Ransom, Cleanth Brooks, Robert Penn Warren, W.K. Wimsatt, Allen Tate — argued that the literary work should be analysed as an autonomous object, separate from its author's biography or its historical moment.

The method was close reading: sustained attention to the actual words, images, ironies, and tensions of the text. Brooks's The Well Wrought Urn (1947) is the canonical demonstration.

The pedagogical effect was enormous. Brooks and Warren's Understanding Poetry textbook (1938) reshaped how generations of American students learned to read.

concepts.title: The Intentional Fallacy
concepts.contentHtml:
Wimsatt and Beardsley's 1946 essay 'The Intentional Fallacy' argued that the author's stated intention is irrelevant — and unknowable — for evaluating a work. What matters is what the work actually does.

The companion essay 'The Affective Fallacy' (1949) argued that the reader's emotional response is similarly inadequate as a guide to meaning.

Both moves were attempts to keep criticism focused on the text rather than dissolving into biography or psychology. The author's life and the reader's reaction were declared methodologically out of bounds.

concepts.title: Russian Formalism
concepts.contentHtml:
Earlier and parallel: Russian Formalism, active roughly 1915-1930. Key figures: Viktor Shklovsky, Roman Jakobson, Yuri Tynyanov, Boris Eikhenbaum.

Their core idea: literature is defined by its literariness — the formal devices that make language literary rather than ordinary. Shklovsky's term ostranenie ('defamiliarisation') named the distinctive effect: literature makes the familiar strange so we see it again.

Russian Formalism was suppressed under Stalin in the 1930s. Many of its insights survived through Jakobson's later work in Prague and the United States, feeding into structuralism.

concepts.title: What New Criticism Got Right
concepts.contentHtml:
Even after later theory dethroned it, New Criticism's contributions remain.

Close reading as discipline: the basic skill of paying sustained attention to words on the page. Without it, criticism becomes opinion.

Pattern recognition: irony, ambiguity, paradox, tension as constitutive of literary meaning, not flaws to be resolved.

Resistance to paraphrase: a poem isn't reducible to a single statement. Cleanth Brooks called this 'the heresy of paraphrase.'

concepts.title: What New Criticism Missed
concepts.contentHtml:
The blind spots that later theory targeted:

History: treating the text as autonomous excluded political and material context. Jameson and other Marxists pushed back hard.

Reader: dismissing reader response left no room for how meaning actually arises in reading. Reception theory (Iser, Jauss) returned to it.

Power: by treating the canon as neutral, New Criticism reinforced existing exclusions. Feminist, postcolonial, and queer criticism exposed this.

The methodological move that excluded politics from criticism was itself political. The next generation made that visible.

title: Structuralism & Post-Structuralism
description: Saussure, Barthes, Derrida — language and meaning

concepts.title: Saussure
concepts.contentHtml:
Ferdinand de Saussure's posthumously published Course in General Linguistics (1916) became the foundation of structuralist thought. His insights:

The linguistic sign has two parts: signifier (sound) and signified (concept). The relation between them is arbitrary.

Meaning is differential: a word means what it does because of what it's not. 'Tree' is what it is by not being shrub, plant, forest.

Language is a system: meaning emerges from the structure of relationships, not from individual words referring to things.

concepts.title: Structuralism
concepts.contentHtml:
Saussure's framework was extended beyond linguistics. Claude Lévi-Strauss applied it to myth (myths share deep structures across cultures). Roland Barthes applied it to fashion, food, professional wrestling, modern advertising — Mythologies (1957) is the canonical example.

The structuralist move: under any cultural surface, find the underlying system of binary oppositions, the deep grammar that generates meaning.

Vladimir Propp's morphology of folktales (covered earlier) was an early structuralist analysis. So was Northrop Frye's Anatomy of Criticism (1957) on literary archetypes.

concepts.title: Derrida and Deconstruction
concepts.contentHtml:
Jacques Derrida's 1967 trio (Of Grammatology, Writing and Difference, Speech and Phenomena) launched deconstruction.

His move against structuralism: every binary opposition the structuralist finds (speech/writing, presence/absence, nature/culture) privileges one term over the other, and every text contains the resources to reverse the privilege. Texts deconstruct themselves.

Derrida's coinage différance (with the deliberate misspelling) holds together two senses: difference (Saussurean) and deferral (meaning never fully arrives, always pointing elsewhere).

The American reception was particularly intense at Yale (Paul de Man, Geoffrey Hartman, J. Hillis Miller). For a decade, deconstruction dominated graduate literary studies.

concepts.title: The Death of the Author
concepts.contentHtml:
Roland Barthes's essay 'The Death of the Author' (1967) was a manifesto for post-structuralist criticism.

His argument: the author is a modern invention. Treating the work as the expression of an author's intention closes off meaning. The reader is the place where meaning happens — and the reader is multiple, historical, always provisional.

The companion essay was Foucault's 'What Is an Author?' (1969), which traced the historical emergence of the 'author function' as a social and legal category.

The arguments freed criticism from biographical reduction. They were also overstated — readers do still care about authors, sometimes for good reasons. But the move shifted critical attention permanently.

concepts.title: After Post-Structuralism
concepts.contentHtml:
By the 1990s the high theoretical wave had ebbed. The vocabulary persists; the grand totalising claims have become quieter.

Contemporary literary studies tends to use post-structuralist insights pragmatically rather than programmatically. Recognition that meaning is unstable, that texts contain internal contradictions, that the author's biography doesn't decide interpretation — these are now baseline assumptions, not contested theses.

The pendulum has swung partly back. Recent decades have seen renewed interest in historical context, biographical specifics, even authorial intention. The post-structuralist phase didn't end; it integrated.

title: Marxist Criticism
description: Lukács, Williams, Jameson — ideology in the text

concepts.title: Marx and Literature
concepts.contentHtml:
Marx didn't write systematic literary criticism. But his materialist framework — that consciousness is shaped by material conditions of production — implied a literary criticism his successors developed.

The basic Marxist claim about literature: works don't float free of class society. They emerge from particular economic structures, encode (often unconsciously) the ideological assumptions of those structures, and serve or contest the interests of particular classes.

Marx and Engels themselves admired Balzac, Shakespeare, Goethe — sophisticated about the relationship of art to its conditions, not crudely reductive.

concepts.title: Lukács
concepts.contentHtml:
Georg Lukács (Hungarian, 1885-1971) was the first major Marxist literary theorist. The Theory of the Novel (1916) and The Historical Novel (1937) are his major works.

His distinction: realism (Balzac, Tolstoy) versus naturalism (Zola, Flaubert). Realism gave a totalising picture of social relations; naturalism reduced people to environmental products. He preferred realism.

Lukács was suspicious of modernism — he saw Joyce and Kafka as symptoms of bourgeois disintegration, not artistic progress. His preferred totalising realism became Soviet socialist-realist orthodoxy, with results he didn't fully endorse.

concepts.title: Frankfurt School Aesthetics
concepts.contentHtml:
The Frankfurt School took Marxist aesthetics in a different direction. Adorno, Horkheimer, Benjamin, Marcuse engaged seriously with modernism rather than dismissing it.

Adorno argued that genuinely difficult modernist art (Schoenberg's atonal music, Beckett's late plays) registers the truth of capitalist society precisely through its difficulty. Easy art reconciles audiences to oppression; hard art refuses reconciliation.

Walter Benjamin's 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' (1936) analysed how new media (photography, film) changed art's social function. The category of 'aura' he introduced has been continuously useful.

concepts.title: Raymond Williams
concepts.contentHtml:
Raymond Williams (1921-1988) developed a distinctively British cultural materialism.

Culture and Society (1958) traced the keyword 'culture' through 19th- and 20th-century English thought. The Country and the City (1973) tracked the literary representation of rural and urban life across centuries, exposing the ideological work the rural-pastoral tradition did for capitalism.

Williams's distinctive contribution was the concept of structures of feeling — the not-yet-articulated emerging worldview of an era, visible in literature before it surfaces in explicit ideology. Useful for thinking about how literature can register social change before social change is named.

concepts.title: Jameson and the Political Unconscious
concepts.contentHtml:
Fredric Jameson's The Political Unconscious (1981) is the major American Marxist literary work of the late 20th century.

His argument: every text encodes — often unconsciously — a fantasy resolution of real social contradictions the society can't actually resolve. Reading literature politically means reading for what the text can't quite say.

Jameson's later Postmodernism, or, the Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism (1991) became a standard reference for diagnosing post-1970s culture. His characteristic moves — totalising historical reading, attention to form as ideology, sympathy for popular culture as well as high — kept Marxist literary criticism alive in the post-Cold-War era.

title: Psychoanalytic Criticism
description: Freud, Lacan, the unconscious of literature

concepts.title: Freud and Literature
concepts.contentHtml:
Freud read literature as a clinical resource. The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) drew on Sophocles and Shakespeare; the Oedipus complex was named after Sophocles's Oedipus.

His distinctive moves for literary criticism: the text encodes unconscious wishes; symbols (often sexual) carry hidden content; resistance and repression operate in artistic creation as in dreams.

Freud's own essays on literature ('The Uncanny,' 1919; 'Dostoevsky and Parricide,' 1928) tend to be reductive in their conclusions but generative in their attention to what texts seem to evade.

concepts.title: Early Psychoanalytic Criticism
concepts.contentHtml:
The first wave applied Freudian concepts to authors and characters. Was Hamlet Oedipal (Ernest Jones, 1949)? Could you analyse Shakespeare himself through his plays?

This 'biographical' psychoanalytic criticism tended to flatten texts to symptoms. Modern readers find it dated.

More productive: Norman Holland's reader-response psychoanalysis (the reader projects unconscious content onto texts) and Marie Bonaparte's study of Poe (1933).

concepts.title: Lacan
concepts.contentHtml:
Jacques Lacan (1901-1981) reformulated psychoanalysis through structuralist linguistics. His famous slogan: 'The unconscious is structured like a language.'

Key concepts: the mirror stage (the infant's misrecognition of itself as unified); the imaginary, symbolic, and real orders; desire as fundamentally about lack rather than fulfilment.

Lacan's writing is notoriously difficult — deliberately so. His seminars (delivered in Paris from the 1950s onward) attracted enormous followings. Slavoj Žižek's contemporary work continues to popularise Lacanian readings of culture.

concepts.title: Object Relations and Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
Other psychoanalytic traditions have shaped literary criticism.

Object relations theory (Klein, Winnicott) emphasises early relationships and fantasy. Adam Phillips's accessible essays bring object-relations sensibility to literary reading.

Trauma theory (Cathy Caruth, Shoshana Felman) reads texts as registering historical traumas (the Holocaust, slavery) the culture can't process directly.

Queer theory (Sedgwick, Butler) draws on psychoanalysis while critiquing its heteronormative assumptions.

concepts.title: What Survives
concepts.contentHtml:
Psychoanalytic literary criticism is less dominant than in the 1970s. The reasons are partly internal (the empirical status of Freudian and Lacanian claims is contested) and partly external (other theoretical frameworks have crowded in).

What survives is the basic intuition: texts know more than they say. The reader can attend to slips, contradictions, repetitions, evasions as carrying meaning the surface doesn't. This is a tool, not a complete method, and most contemporary critics use it occasionally rather than systematically.

concepts.title: First-Wave Feminist Criticism
concepts.contentHtml:
Feminist literary criticism began with two questions: where are the women writers, and how have men represented women?

Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own (1929) anticipated the field. Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex (1949) gave it philosophical foundations.

In the 1970s the project accelerated. Kate Millett's Sexual Politics (1970) read Mailer, Lawrence, Miller for misogyny. Elaine Showalter's A Literature of Their Own (1977) recovered British women novelists. Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar's The Madwoman in the Attic (1979) reread the 19th-century women's tradition.

concepts.title: Gynocriticism
concepts.contentHtml:
Gynocriticism (Showalter's term) focuses on women writers as their own tradition. The recovery project — finding lost women novelists, poets, dramatists — has been one of literary studies' most productive enterprises.

Major recoveries: Aphra Behn (17th-century playwright and novelist), Margaret Cavendish, Sarah Fielding, Anne Brontë (long overshadowed by her sisters), Charlotte Mew, Mina Loy, Zora Neale Hurston (whose 1937 Their Eyes Were Watching God was rediscovered in the 1970s).

The recovery has reshaped the canon. Anthologies that included one or two women writers in 1970 routinely include thirty or forty now.

concepts.title: French Feminism
concepts.contentHtml:
The French strand emphasised psychoanalysis and language.

Hélène Cixous's 'The Laugh of the Medusa' (1975) called for écriture féminine — a writing that would express female experience differently from patriarchal language.

Luce Irigaray's Speculum of the Other Woman (1974) read Western philosophy from Plato onward as systematically excluding the feminine.

Julia Kristeva (covered earlier for intertextuality) developed the concept of the semiotic — pre-linguistic, maternal, disruptive — against the symbolic order of patriarchal language.

concepts.title: Sedgwick and Queer Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick's Between Men (1985) and Epistemology of the Closet (1990) launched queer theory as a major field.

Her arguments: male homosocial bonds in literature have homoerotic dimensions the texts both display and disavow. The closet — the structure of knowing-but-not-saying — shapes Western culture far beyond the explicitly homosexual.

Judith Butler's Gender Trouble (1990) extended the analysis. Gender, on her account, is performative — produced through repeated acts rather than expressing a prior essence. The argument has been hugely influential well beyond literary studies.

concepts.title: Intersectionality and Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
Black feminist criticism — Barbara Smith, bell hooks, Hortense Spillers — exposed the racial blind spots of mainstream feminist theory.

Kimberlé Crenshaw's term intersectionality (1989) became the standard vocabulary for analysing how race, gender, class, and sexuality interact rather than operating separately.

Contemporary feminist and gender criticism integrates intersectional, queer, and trans theoretical work. The field is no longer organised around a unified 'feminism' but around overlapping critical projects all attentive to gendered, racialised, sexualised power.

title: Reader Response & Reception
description: Iser, Jauss — meaning in the act of reading

concepts.title: Bringing the Reader Back
concepts.contentHtml:
New Criticism had banished the reader as a source of meaning ('the affective fallacy'). Reader-response criticism, developed in the 1960s and 70s, brought the reader back as central.

The basic claim: meaning isn't in the text alone. It arises in the encounter between text and reader. Different readers — and the same reader at different moments — produce different readings, all of them potentially valid.

The move was American (Stanley Fish, Norman Holland) and German (the Constance School: Wolfgang Iser, Hans Robert Jauss). Both lines pushed back against text-only formalism.

concepts.title: Iser and Indeterminacy
concepts.contentHtml:
Wolfgang Iser's The Implied Reader (1974) and The Act of Reading (1976) developed the most systematic reader-response theory.

Iser argued that texts contain gaps and indeterminacies — points where the reader must fill in, infer, complete. A novel says some things; it leaves others for the reader to construct. Reading is an active process of filling.

The 'implied reader' is the reader the text positions and instructs — not a real reader, but the role the text invites real readers to occupy.

concepts.title: Jauss and Reception
concepts.contentHtml:
Hans Robert Jauss's 'Literary History as a Challenge to Literary Theory' (1967) launched reception aesthetics.

His central concept: the horizon of expectations. Each historical period's readers approach texts with shared assumptions — about genre, character, moral framework. A text either confirms those expectations or challenges them.

The same text can challenge expectations at one moment and confirm them at another. Madame Bovary scandalised 1857 readers; later generations read it as classical realism. Reception history tracks how horizons shift.

concepts.title: Stanley Fish
concepts.contentHtml:
The American counterpart was Stanley Fish. His Is There a Text in This Class? (1980) collected essays developing the concept of interpretive communities.

His argument: meaning isn't in the text or in the individual reader. It's in the shared interpretive practices of the community the reader belongs to. A 1950s New Critic and a 1980s deconstructionist read the same words differently because they belong to different communities of practice.

The argument was provocative and influential. It's been criticised for relativism, but the basic insight — that what counts as a valid reading depends on community standards — has been hard to refute.

concepts.title: After Reader Response
concepts.contentHtml:
Reader-response theory faded as a distinct movement by the late 1980s, but its insights have been absorbed.

Contemporary scholarship is much more attentive to actual reading practices than 1960s formalism was. The history of reading — what readers actually did with texts in earlier periods — is now an active sub-field.

Empirical reader research, drawing on cognitive science and digital reading platforms, has begun supplementing theoretical reader-response work. We can now study how real readers process texts in measurable ways.

The category of 'the reader' is permanent in literary studies now. It returned because it had to.
